2891.sol:
Statements (i) and (iii) are not correct. Their correct explanation are as follows:
(i) According to VSEPR theory \($\mathrm{ClF}}_{3}\) has 3 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs thus it is \(A B_3 E_2\) type molecule whereas \( \mathrm{SO}$}_{2}\) has \(2 $\sigma$\) bond pairs and one lone pair so it is \(A B_2 E\) type molecule.
(iii) \($\mathrm{HgCl}}_{2}\) has a linear shape because it has 2 bond pairs only whereas \( \mathrm{PbCl}$}_{2}\) has 2 bond pairs with one lone pair thus it has a bent shape.

5440.sol:
Let's take the equal weights of the three isotopes as $2 g$.
$\Rightarrow \mathrm{n}_1=1 \mathrm{ mol}, \mathrm{n}_2=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{ mol}, \mathrm{n}_3=\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{ mol}\mathrm{n}_{\text{total }}=1+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{11}{6}\Rightarrow x_1=\frac{1}{\frac{11}{6}}=0.54, x_2=\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{11}{6}}=0.27, x_3=\frac{\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{11}{6}}=0.18$
From Dalton's law of partial pressures:-
$\begin{aligned}
& P_i=x_i P_{\text{total }} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{P_3}{P_2}=\frac{x_3 P}{x_2 P}=\frac{0.18}{0.27} \text{ and } \frac{P_2}{P_1}=\frac{x_2}{x_1}=\frac{0.27}{0.54} \\
& \Rightarrow P_3: P_2: P_1=0.18: 0.27: 0.54
\end{aligned}$

$f\left(x\right) = 2x^{2} - logx$

Function is decreasing when $f^{'}\left(x\right) < 0$

$4x - \dfrac{1}{x} < 0$

$⇒ 4x^{2} - 1 < 0$

$⇒ x^{2} < \dfrac{1}{4}$

$⇒ x \in \left(- \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right).$

But, $x > 0$

Therefore, $f \left(x\right)$ is decreasing when$x \in \left(0, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.$

7138.text: If the angle between the circles $x^2+y^2-2 x-4 y+c=0$ and $x^2+y^2-4 x-2 y+4=0$ is $60^{{}^{\circ}}$, then $c$ is equal to
7138.sol:
We have,
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{C}_1: x^2+y^2-2 x-4 y+c=0 ... (i)\\
& \mathrm{C}_2: x^2+y^2-4 x-2 y+4=0... (ii)
\end{aligned}$
So, centre of circle $\mathrm{C}_1=(1,2), r_1=\sqrt{5-c}$ and centre of circle $\mathrm{C}_2=(2,1), r_2=1$
Now, angle between the two circles,
$\begin{aligned}
\cos \theta & =\frac{\left(\mathrm{C}_1 \mathrm{C}_2\right)^2-\left(r_1^2+r_2^2\right)}{2 r_1 r_2} \\
\cos \theta & =\frac{\left[(2-1)^2+(1-2)^2\right]-(5-c+1)}{2 \sqrt{5}-c(1)}
\end{aligned}$
Given, $\theta=60^{{}^{\circ}}\begin{aligned}
& \cos 60^{{}^{\circ}}=\frac{1+1-5+c-1}{2 \sqrt{5-c}} \\
& \frac{1}{2}=\frac{c-4}{2 \sqrt{5-c}} \\
& \sqrt{5-c}=c-4
\end{aligned}$
On squaring both sides, we get
$\begin{aligned}
& 5-c=c^2-8 c+16 \\
& c^2-5 c+11=0 \\
& c=\frac{7 \pm \sqrt{49-44}}{2} \\
& c=\frac{7 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}
\end{aligned}$

7392.text: Let the complex numbers \($\alpha$ and \($\left(\frac{1}{\bar{\alpha}}\right)$ lie on circles \($\left(x-x_0\right)^2+$\left(y-y_0\right)^2=r²\)$ and \(\left(x-x_0\right)^2+\left(y-y_0\right)^2=4$ r²\) respectively. If \(z_0=x_0+i y_0\) satisfies the $equation \(2\left|$z_0\right|^2=\) \(r²+2\), then \(|$\alpha|=$
7392.sol:
As point $\alpha\) lies on the circle
\begin{aligned}& \left(x-x_0\right)^2+\left(y-y_0\right)^2 =r² \\
\therefore & \left|\alpha-z_0\right|^2=r², \text{ where }z_0 =x_0+i y_0 \\
\Rightarrow & |\alpha|^2+\left|z_0\right|^2-\left(\alpha \bar{z}_0+\bar{\alpha} z_0\right) =r² \quad \ldots (i)
\end{aligned}\)
\(\because \frac{1}{\bar{\alpha}}\) lies on the circle \(\left(x-x_0\right)^2+\left(y-y_0\right)^2=4 r²\)
\(\therefore \quad\left|\frac{1}{\bar{\alpha}}-z_0\right|^2=4 r²\)
\begin{aligned}& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{|\alpha|^2}+\left|z_0\right|^2-\left(\frac{\alpha \bar{z}_0}{|\alpha|^2}+\frac{\bar{\alpha} z_0}{|\alpha|^2}\right)=4 r² \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 1+\left|z_0\right|^2|\alpha|^2-\left(\alpha \bar{z}_0+\bar{\alpha} z_0\right)=4 r²|\alpha|^2 \quad \ldots (ii)
\end{aligned}\)
By subtracting Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
\begin{array}{cc}& 1-|\alpha|^2-\left|z_0\right|^2\left(1-|\alpha|^2\right)=r²\left(4|\alpha|^2-1\right) \\
\Rightarrow & \left(|\alpha|^2-1\right)\left(\left|z_0\right|^2-1\right)=r²\left(4|\alpha|^2-1\right) \\
\because & \left|z_0\right|^2=\frac{r^2+2}{2}, \text{ we get }
\end{array}
\begin{aligned}& \left(|\alpha|^2-1\right) \frac{r^2}{2} =r^2\left(4|\alpha|^2-1\right) \\
\Rightarrow & |\alpha|^2-1 =8|\alpha|^2-2 \\
\Rightarrow & 7|\alpha|^2=1 \Rightarrow|\alpha| =\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}
\end{aligned}$

7597.text:
If a function \(f\) is defined by :
\begin{aligned} f(x) & =0, $\text{ when }$x=1, \\
& =x³-1, $\text{ when }$1 < x < \infty,

7597.sol:
We have,
\(f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{rc}
x-1, & -\infty  < x <  1 \\
0, & x=1 \\
x³-1, & 1 <  x <  \infty
\end{array}\right.\)
Now, (LHL at \(x=1\) )
\(\begin{aligned}
& =\lim _{x \rightarrow 1}(x-1) \\
& =\mathbf{l}-\mathbf{l}=\mathbf{0}
\end{aligned}\)
(RHL at \(x=1\) ) \(=\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} x^3-1\)
\(=(\mathrm{l})^3-\mathbf{1}=0 \text{ and } f(\mathrm{l})=0\)
\(\therefore \quad \text{ LHL }=\text{ RHL }= f(\mathrm{l})\)
So, \(f(x)\) is continuous at \(x=1\)
Now, (LHD at \(x=1\) )
\(=\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{(x-1)-0}{x-1}=1\)
and (RHD at \(x=1\) )
\(\begin{aligned}
& =\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{\left(x^3-1\right)-0}{x-1}\\
& =\lim _{x \rightarrow 1}\left(x^2+x+1\right)=3
\end{aligned}\)
\(\therefore\) LHD \( ≠ \) RHD
So, \(f(x)\) is not differentiable at \(x=1\)

16017.text: A body of mass $4.9 \mathrm{ kg}$ hangs from a spring and oscillates with a period $0.5 \mathrm{ s}$. On the removal of the body, the spring is shortened by (take, $g=10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}, \pi^2=10$ )
16017.sol:
Given that, mass of body, $m=4.9 \mathrm{ kg}$
Time period of oscillation of spring,
$T=0.5 \mathrm{ s}$
Acceleration due to gravity, $g=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2
and \pi^2=10$
We know that, time period of spring
$T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$
By squaring on both sides, $T^2=4 \pi^2 \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{k}}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{m}{k}=\frac{T^2}{4 \pi^2}=\frac{(0.5)^2}{4 \times 10}=\frac{0.25}{40}=0.00625$
After removal of mass, length of spring decrease is equal to extension produced in spring.
By using equilibrium condition,
$F=m g\Rightarrow \quad k x=m gx=\frac{m}{k} g$
Substituting the values, we get
$\begin{aligned} x & =0.00625 \times 10 \\ & =0.0625 \mathrm{ m} \\ & =6.25 \mathrm{ cm}\end{aligned}$
Hence, the spring is shortened by $6.25 \mathrm{ cm}$ after removal of mass.

21831.text: On each working day of a school there are six periods. The number of ways in which five subjects are arranged if each subject is allotted at least one period and no period remains vacant is
21831.sol:
There are 6 periods and 5 subjects. Each subject must be allotted at least one period. Since there are 6 periods and 5 subjects, exactly one subject must be allotted two periods, and the remaining four subjects must be allotted one period each.

First, choose the subject that will be allotted two periods. This can be done in ^{5}C_{1} = 5$ ways.

Next, choose the two periods out of 6 that will be assigned to this subject. This can be done in ^{6}C_{2} = 15$ ways.

The remaining 4 periods are to be assigned to the remaining 4 subjects in $4!$ ways.

The total number of ways is $5 \times 15 \times 4! = 75 \times 24 = 1800$.

Answer: 1800

The coordinates of $P$ are given by the section formula:

$P = \left( \dfrac{6k + 3}{k + 1}, \dfrac{3k + 5}{k + 1}, \dfrac{-2k - 1}{k + 1} \right)

Given that the $y$-coordinate of $P$ is 2$, we set the $y$-component equal to $2$:

$\dfrac{3k + 5}{k + 1} =2$

3k + 5 = 2(k + 1)$

$3k + 5 = 2k + 2$

$k = -3$

Now, substitute $k = -3$ into the expression for the $x$-coordinate of $P$:

$x = $\dfrac{6(-3) + 3}{-3 + 1}$

$ x = \dfrac{-18 + 3}{-2}$

$ x = \dfrac{-15}{-2} = \dfrac{15}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{15}{2}$

22566.text: In the given circuit, an ideal voltmeter connected across $6\Omega$ reads 5V. The internal resistance r of each cell is:
22566.sol:
The equivalent resistance of the upper branch is $9\ \Omega + 3\ \Omega = 12\ \Omega$.

The equivalent resistance of the parallel combination is $R_p = \dfrac{12 \times 6}{12 + 6} = 4\ \Omega$.

The voltage across the parallel combination is given as $V_p = 5\text{ V}$.

The main circuit current is $I = \dfrac{V_p}{R_p} = \dfrac{5}{4} = 1.25\text{ A}$.

The total external resistance is $R_{\text{ext}} = 2 + 4 = 6\ \Omega$.

The total EMF of the circuit is $E = 4 + 4 = 8\text{ V}$ and total internal resistance is $2r$.

Applying Ohm's law for the complete circuit:

$I = \dfrac{E}{R_{\text{ext}} + 2r}$

$1.25 = \dfrac{8}{6 + 2r}$

$6 + 2r = \dfrac{8}{1.25} = 6.4$

$2r = 0.4 \Rightarrow r = 0.2\ \Omega$

Answer: $0.2\ \Omega$

23011.subject: Physics
23011.text: In to a uniform transverse magnetic field, two charged particles having the same mass and charge enter and move in two different circular paths. The ratio of the radii of curvatures of the circular paths is $1: 4$. What would be the ratio of their respective velocities?
23011.sol:
The radius $r$ of the circular path of a charged particle moving in a uniform transverse magnetic field $B$ is given by the formula $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$, where $m$ is the mass, $v$ is the velocity, and $q$ is the charge of the particle.

Given that the mass $m$ and charge $q$ are the same for both particles, and the magnetic field $B$ is uniform, the radius $r$ is directly proportional to the velocity $v$. That is, $r \propto v$.

Therefore, the ratio of the radii of the two circular paths is equal to the ratio of their respective velocities:

$\dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2}$

Given that the ratio of the radii is $1: 4$, we have:

$\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Thus, the ratio of their respective velocities is $1: 4$.

Answer: $\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}=1: 4$

25728.text: Let $X = \left\{\left(x, y\right) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}: \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{8} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{20} < 1and{y}^{2} < 5x\right\}$. Three distinct point $P, Q$ and $R$ are randomly chosen from $X$. Then the probability that $P, Q$ and $R$ form a triangle whose area is a positive integer, is
25728.sol:
Given,

Equation of ellipse $\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{8} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{20} = 1$

And equation of parabola ${y}^{2} = 5x$

Now intersection point of ellipse and parabola will be $\left(2, \sqrt{10}\right) \text{ and } \left(2, - \sqrt{10}\right)$

Now plotting the region $\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{8} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{20} < 1and{y}^{2} < 5x$ we get,

Now randomly chosen points will be between origin and the intersecting point,

So, the integer points inside region are $\left\{\left(2, 1\right), \left(2, - 1\right), \left(2, 2\right), \left(2, - 2\right), \left(2, 3\right), \left(2, - 3\right), \left(2, 0\right), \left(1, 1\right), \left(1, - 1\right), \left(1, 2\right), \left(1, - 2\right), \left(1, 0\right)\right\}$

Total number of ways to select three points $= C3 12 = 220$

Required number of triangle $= 4 \times C1 7 + 9 \times C1 5 = 73$

{Note: Points are taken such a way that distance between two points are multiple of $2$ for example if we take points on line $x = 1$ we can take following points $\left\{\left(1, 2\right) \text{ and } \left(1, 0\right), \left(1, 0\right) \text{ and } \left(1, - 2\right), \left(1, 1\right) \text{ and } \left(1, - 1\right), \left(1, 2\right) \text{ and } \left(1, - 2\right)\right\}$

so there will be $4$ pairs from line $x = 1$ and will chose another point from $x = 2$ line so triangle will have a positive area. Also note that height of the triangle will always be $1$}

Hence, probability will be $= \dfrac{73}{220}$

25980.text: Let $\overset{\to}{a}, \overset{\to}{b}$ and $\overset{\to}{c}$ be three non - coplanar unit vectors such that the angle between every pair of them is $\dfrac{\pi}{3} .$ If $\overset{\to}{a} \times \overset{\to}{b} + \overset{\to}{b} \times \overset{\to}{c} = p\overset{\to}{a} + q\overset{\to}{b} + r\overset{\to}{c}$ , where p, q and r are scalars, then the value of $\dfrac{{p}^{2} + 2{q}^{2} + {r}^{2}}{{q}^{2}}$ is _______
25980.sol:
$\left|\overset{\to}{a}\right| = \left|\overset{\to}{b}\right| = \left|\overset{\to}{c}\right| = 1$
$\overset{\to}{a} \times \overset{\to}{b} + \overset{\to}{b} \times \overset{\to}{c} = p\overset{\to}{a} + q\overset{\to}{b} + r\overset{\to}{c}$
$\overset{\to}{a} . \left(\overset{\to}{b} \times \overset{\to}{c}\right) = p + q\left(\overset{\to}{a} . \overset{\to}{b}\right) + r\left(\overset{\to}{a} . \overset{\to}{c}\right)$
And $\left[\overset{\to}{a}\overset{\to}{b}\overset{\to}{c}\right] = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
$p + \dfrac{q}{2} + \dfrac{r}{2} = \left[\overset{\to}{a}\overset{\to}{b}\overset{\to}{c}\right]$ .......(i)
$\dfrac{p}{2} + q + \dfrac{r}{2} = 0$ ......(ii)
$\dfrac{p}{2} + \dfrac{q}{2} + r = \left[\overset{\to}{a}\overset{\to}{b}\overset{\to}{c}\right]$ ......(iii)
$⇒$ $p = r = - q$
$\dfrac{{p}^{2} + 2{q}^{2} + {r}^{2}}{{q}^{2}} = 4$

Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion and the other is labelled as Reason.

Assertion: The ionic radii of ${O}^{2 -}$ and ${Mg}^{2 +}$ are same.

$\dfrac{z}{e}of{Mg}^{2 +} = \dfrac{12}{10} = 1 . 2$

$\dfrac{z}{e} = \dfrac{Numberofprotons}{Numberofelectrons}$

If the same buffer was used in the following electrochemical cell to record a cell potential of $235.3\,\mathrm{mV}$, then the value of $x = \_\_\_\_$ mL (nearest integer).

$\mathrm{Sn(s)} \; \big| \; \mathrm{Sn(OH)_6^{2-}}(0.5\,\mathrm{M}) \; \big| \; \mathrm{HSnO_2^-}(0.05\,\mathrm{M}) \; \big| \; \mathrm{OH^-} \; \big| \; \mathrm{Bi_2O_3(s)} \; \big| \; \mathrm{Bi(s)}$

Consider up to one place of decimal for intermediate calculations.

$\begin{array}{ll}\text{Given:} & E^\circ_{\mathrm{[Sn(OH)_6]^{2-}/HSnO_2^-}} = -0.90\,\mathrm{V} \\[4pt]& E^\circ_{\mathrm{Bi_2O_3/Bi}} = -0.44\,\mathrm{V} \\[4pt]& \mathrm{p}K_a(\mathrm{H_2CO_3}) = 6.11 \\[4pt]& \dfrac{2.303\,RT}{F} = 0.059\,\mathrm{V} \\[6pt]& \text{Antilog}(1.29) = 19.5\end{array}$

32175.subject: Chemistry
32175.text: The energy required by electrons, present in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen atom to be excited to second Bohr orbit is $\_\_\_\_$ $\mathrm{J} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$. Given: $R_{H}=2.18 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{ergs}$.
32175.sol:
The energy of an electron in the $n^{th}$ Bohr orbit of a hydrogen atom is given by $E_n = -R_H \left( \frac{1}{n^2} \right)$.
The energy required for excitation from $n=1$ to $n=2$ for a single atom is $\Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = R_H \left( \frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{2^2} \right) = R_H \left( 1 - \frac{1}{4} \right) = \frac{3}{4} R_H$.
Given $R_H = 2.18 \times 10^{-11}$ ergs.
Converting ergs to Joules: $1 \text{ erg} = 10^{-7} \text{ J}$.
So, $R_H = 2.18 \times 10^{-11} \times 10^{-7} = 2.18 \times 10^{-18} \text{ J}$.
The energy required per atom is $\Delta E = \frac{3}{4} \times 2.18 \times 10^{-18} = 1.635 \times 10^{-18} \text{ J}$.
To find the energy required per mole of electrons, multiply by Avogadro's number $N_A \approx 6.022 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$.
Energy per mole $= 1.635 \times 10^{-18} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \text{ J mol}^{-1}$.
Energy per mole $\approx 9.846 \times 10^5 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$.
Comparing with the given options, $9.835 \times 10^5$ is the closest value.

34796.subject: Mathematics
34796.text: Let $y = y ( x )$ be the solution of the differential equation $cosx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 ) dy = ( 1 + ysinx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 ) ) dx, 0 \le x \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}, y\left(0\right) = 0 .$ Then, $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ is equal to:
34796.sol:
Given $cosx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 ) dy = ( 1 + ysinx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 ) ) dx$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{( 1 + ysinx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 ) )}{cosx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 )}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{cosx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 )} + \dfrac{ysinx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 ) )}{cosx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 )}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} - ( tanx ) y = \dfrac{1}{( 3sinx + cosx + 3 ) cosx}$

This is a linear differential equation of the type $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q,$ where $P = - tanx$ and $Q = \dfrac{1}{cosx\left(3sinx + cosx + 3\right)} .$

Now, the integrating factor $I . F . = {e}^{∫ Pdx} = {e}^{∫ - tanxdx}$

$= {e}^{ln\left|cosx\right|} = \left|cosx\right|$

$= cosx ∀ 0 \le x \le \dfrac{\pi}{2} .$

The solution of the given differential equation is $y\left(I . F .\right) = ∫ Q\left(I . F .\right)dx + C$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = ∫ ( cosx ) \cdot \dfrac{1}{cosx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 )}dx + C$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = ∫ \dfrac{dx}{3sinx + cosx + 3}dx + C$

Using $sin2\theta = \dfrac{2tan\theta}{1 + \tan^{2}\theta} \text{ and } cos2\theta = \dfrac{1 - \tan^{2}\theta}{1 + \tan^{2}\theta}$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = ∫ \dfrac{1}{3 \times \dfrac{2tan\dfrac{x}{2}}{1 + \tan^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}} + \dfrac{1 - \tan^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}}{1 + \tan^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}} + 3}dx + C$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = ∫ \dfrac{1 + \tan^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}}{6tan\dfrac{x}{2} + 1 - \tan^{2}\dfrac{x}{2} + 3 + 3\tan^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}}dx + C$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = ∫ \dfrac{\left({sec}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}{2\tan^{2}\dfrac{x}{2} + 6tan\dfrac{x}{2} + 4}dx + C$

Let ${I}_{1} = ∫ \dfrac{\left({sec}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}{2\left(\tan^{2}\dfrac{x}{2} + 3tan\dfrac{x}{2} + 2\right)}dx + C$

Put $tan\dfrac{x}{2} = t ⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}{sec}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}dx = dt$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = ∫ \dfrac{dt}{{t}^{3} + 3t + 2} = ∫ \dfrac{dt}{\left(t + 2\right) ( t + 1 )}$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = ∫ \left(\dfrac{1}{t + 1} - \dfrac{1}{t + 2}\right)dt$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = {\log}_{e}\left(t + 1\right) - {\log}_{e}\left(t + 2\right)$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = {\log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{t + 1}{t + 2}\right)$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = {\log}_{e}\left|\left(\dfrac{tan\dfrac{x}{2} + 1}{tan\dfrac{x}{2} + 2}\right)\right|$

So, the solution is $y\left(cosx\right) = {\log}_{e}\left|\dfrac{1 + tan\dfrac{x}{2}}{2 + tan\dfrac{x}{2}}\right| + C$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = {\log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{1 + tan\dfrac{x}{2}}{2 + tan\dfrac{x}{2}}\right) + C$ for $0 \le x \le \dfrac{\pi}{2} .$

Now, it is given $y ( 0 ) = 0$

$⇒ 0 = {\log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + C ⇒ C = {\log}_{e}2$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = {\log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{1 + tan\dfrac{x}{2}}{2 + tan\dfrac{x}{2}}\right) + {\log}_{e}2$

Now, for $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3},$ $y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = {\log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{2 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}\right) + {\log}_{e}2$

$⇒ y \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = {\log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{2\sqrt{3} + 1}\right) + {\log}_{e}2$

$⇒ y \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = {\log}_{e}\left(\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{2\sqrt{3} + 1}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{3} - 1}{2\sqrt{3} - 1}\right)\right) + {\log}_{e}2$

$⇒ y \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = {\log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{5 + \sqrt{3}}{11}\right) + {\log}_{e}2$

$⇒ y = 2{\log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{3} + 10}{11}\right) .$

Given differential equation, $ydx - xdy - 3{y}^{2}dy = 0$

$⇒ \dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{x}{y} + 3y$

$\dfrac{dx}{dy} - \dfrac{x}{y} = 3y$

I.F. = ${e}^{- ∫ \dfrac{1}{y}dy} = {e}^{- ln ⁡ y} = \dfrac{1}{y}$

$∴$ solution is

$\dfrac{x}{y} = ∫ 3y . \dfrac{1}{y}dy$

$⇒ \dfrac{x}{y} = 3y + c$

Passes through $( 1, 1 )$,

$∴ 1 = 3 + c; c = - 2$

Equation of required curve, $x = 3{y}^{2} - 2y$

Clearly, it passes through $\left(\dfrac{- 1}{3}, \dfrac{1}{3}\right)$.

39646.text: The resistance of a wire is $5Ω$. Its new resistance in ohm, if stretched to $5$ times of its original length will be :
39646.sol:
The resistance of a wire $( R )$ is related to its resistivity $\left(ρ\right)$, length$( l )$ and cross-sectional area $\left(A\right)$ as:

$R = ρ\dfrac{l}{A}$

As the length of wire increases, the cross-sectional area decreases. The cross-sectional area in terms of volume $( V )$ and length $( l )$ is

$A = \dfrac{V}{l}$

$∴ R = ρ\dfrac{{l}^{2}}{V}$

Taking the volume of wire constant,

$R ∝ {l}^{2}$

So if ${R}^{'}$ is the resistance of wire after getting redrawn and $R$ is the initial resistance of wire,

$∴ \dfrac{{R}^{'}}{R} = \dfrac{( 5l{)}^{2}}{{l}^{2}} = 25 ⇒ {R}^{'} = 25 \times R = 125Ω$

40142.text:
Regarding self-inductance:
A. The self-inductance of the coil depends on its geometry.
B. Self-inductance does not depend on the permeability of the medium.
C. Self-induced e.m.f. opposes any change in the current in a circuit.
D. Self-inductance is electromagnetic analogue of mass in mechanics.
E. Work needs to be done against self-induced e.m.f. in establishing the current.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
40142.sol:
A. The self-inductance of the coil depends on its geometry.
This is true because the self-inductance of a coil is given by formulas that include its geometrical parameters (number of turns, cross-sectional area, length, etc.). For example, for a solenoid,
\(L=\mu_0 \mu_r \frac{N^2 A}{l}\)
where \(N\) is the number of turns, \(A\) is the cross-sectional area, and \(l\) is the length.
B. Self-inductance does not depend on the permeability of the medium.
This is false. The permeability of the medium (represented by \(\mu=\mu_0 \mu_r\)) directly influences the inductance, as seen in the formula above. So, any change in the medium's permeability will affect the inductance.
C. Self-induced e.m.f. opposes any change in the current in a circuit.
This is true, and it is a direct consequence of Lenz's law. The induced electromotive force (e.m.f.) always acts in a direction such that it opposes the change in current that produced it.
D. Self-inductance is the electromagnetic analogue of mass in mechanics.
This is true. Just as mass resists changes in velocity (inertia), inductance resists changes in current, which is why it is often compared to the inertial mass in mechanical systems.
E. Work needs to be done against self-induced e.m.f. in establishing the current.
This is true because, when you try to change the current, you must do work to overcome the opposing self-induced e.m.f., storing energy in the magnetic field of the inductor. Based on the above reasoning, the true statements are \(\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D}\), and E.
Thus, the correct answer is:
Option C
A, C, D, E only

42426.text: A ball is spun with angular acceleration $\alpha = 6{t}^{2} - 2t$ where $t$ is in second and $\alpha$ is in $rad{s}^{- 2}$. Integrating the above,

$⇒ \omega - 10 = 2{t}^{3} - {t}^{2}$

Now, $\omega = \dfrac{d \theta}{d t} = 10 + 2{t}^{3} - {t}^{2}$

${∫}_{4}^{\theta} d \theta = {∫}_{0}^{t}\left(10 + 2{t}^{3} - {t}^{2}\right) d t$

Integrating the above relation,

$\theta - 4 = 10t + \dfrac{{t}^{4}}{2} - \dfrac{{t}^{3}}{3}$

Thus, angular position of the ball is $\theta = \dfrac{{t}^{4}}{2} - \dfrac{{t}^{3}}{3} + 10t + 4$.

42660.subject: Physics
42660.text: The velocity of a particle executing simple harmonic motion along $x$-axis is described as $v^2 = 50 - x^2$, where $x$ represents displacement. If the time period of motion is $\dfrac{x}{7}$ s, the value of $x$ is _____.
42660.sol:
The given equation is $v^2 = 50 - x^2$

Differentiating with respect to $x$:

$2v \dfrac{dv}{dx} = -2x$

$v \dfrac{dv}{dx} = -x$

Since acceleration $a = v \dfrac{dv}{dx}$, we get:

$a = -x$

Comparing this with the standard equation of SHM $a = -\omega^2 x$, we get:

$\omega^2 = 1 \Rightarrow \omega = 1$ rad/s

The time period of the motion is given by:

$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi$

Taking $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, we get:

$T = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} = \dfrac{44}{7}$ s

Given that the time period is $\dfrac{x}{7}$ s, comparing the two gives:

$x = 44$

Answer: $44$

52354.text: A point particle is acted upon by a restoring force $- kx^{3}.$ The time period of oscillation is $T$ when the amplitude is $A.$ The time period for an amplitude $2A$ will be:

Put $\dfrac{x}{A} = u ⇒ dx = Adu$

$T = 4\sqrt{\dfrac{2m}{k}}{A}^{- 1} ( I )$
Where $I = {∫}_{0}^{1}{\left(1 - {u}^{4}\right)}^{- 1 / 2}du$ is a numerical value
So from above equation $T ∝ {A}^{- 1}$
$∴ \dfrac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}} = \dfrac{2A}{A} ⇒ {T}_{2} = \dfrac{T}{2}$

55494.text: Identify the pair of carbohydrates containing galactose as one of constituent in both of them.
55494.sol:
Sucrose is a disaccharide comprising $\alpha$-D-glucose and $\beta$-D-fructose, lacking galactose.

Maltose consists of two $\alpha$-D-glucose units and does not contain galactose.

Lactose contains $\beta$-D-galactose and $\alpha$-D-glucose, hence it includes galactose.

Raffinose is a trisaccharide with D-galactose, D-glucose, and D-fructose; it contains galactose.

Stachyose is a tetrasaccharide composed of two D-galactose, one D-glucose, and one D-fructose, thus containing galactose.

Evaluating option pairs: Raffinose and Stachyose both incorporate galactose, making this the correct pair.

The answer is $\boxed{C}$.

57614.subject: Chemistry
57614.text: What type of arenes are obtained when arene diazonium chloride is treated with fluoroboric acid and then heated further?
57614.sol:
The reaction is the Balz-Schiemann reaction, which synthesizes fluoroarenes from arene diazonium salts.

Arenediazonium fluoroborate forms when arenediazonium chloride $\mathrm{ArN_2^+Cl^-}$ reacts with fluoroboric acid $\mathrm{HBF_4}$:

$\mathrm{ArN_2^+Cl^- + HBF_4 \to ArN_2^+BF_4^- + HCl}$

Thermal decomposition of arenediazonium fluoroborate produces fluoroarene $\mathrm{ArF}$, nitrogen gas, and boron trifluoride:

$\mathrm{ArN_2^+BF_4^- \xrightarrow{heat} ArF + N_2 \uparrow + BF_3}$

The product is a fluoroarene $\mathrm{ArF}$, corresponding to option B.

57756.subject: Chemistry
57756.text: Alkenes on oxidation with $\text{KMnO}_4$ in dil $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ forms
57756.sol:
Alkenes undergo oxidative cleavage when treated with a strong oxidizing agent like $\text{KMnO}_4$ in acidic medium (dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$).

During this reaction, the carbon-carbon double bond is completely cleaved. A $=\text{CH}-$ group is initially oxidized to an aldehyde (alkanal), which is highly susceptible to further oxidation under these conditions and immediately oxidizes to a carboxylic acid (alkanoic acid).

For example:
$\text{R}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{R}' \xrightarrow{\text{KMnO}_4 / \text{H}^+} \text{R}-\text{COOH} + \text{R}'-\text{COOH}$

Thus, the final stable product formed is an alkanoic acid.

Answer: Alkanoic acid

58812.text: Find the volume occupied by a particle in a simple cubic unit cell if the radius of a particle in it is 190 pm.
58812.sol:
The volume occupied by a particle is the volume of the spherical particle itself.

Given the radius of the particle, $r = 190 \text{ pm} = 190 \times 10^{-10} \text{ cm} = 1.9 \times 10^{-8} \text{ cm}$.

Volume of one particle is given by:

$V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$

Substituting the value of $r$:

$V = \dfrac{4}{3} \times 3.1416 \times (1.9 \times 10^{-8} \text{ cm})^3$

$V = 4.1888 \times 6.859 \times 10^{-24} \text{ cm}^3$

$V = 28.73 \times 10^{-24} \text{ cm}^3 = 2.873 \times 10^{-23} \text{ cm}^3$

Answer: $2.873 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{cm}^3$

59554.text: A container contains $4 \mathrm{ g}\mathrm{H}_2, 4 \mathrm{ g}\mathrm{He}$ and certain amount of ' Ne ' at a certain temperature. What is the mass of 'Ne' required so that the partial pressure exerted by ' Ne ' is equal to the partial pressure of He ?
59554.sol:
Dalton's Law implies that partial pressures are equal when mole fractions are equal, which requires equal numbers of moles for gases in the same container at constant temperature.

Given $4\ \mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{H_2}$ ($M = 2\ \mathrm{g/mol}$) and $4\ \mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{He}$ ($M = 4\ \mathrm{g/mol}$), the moles are $n_{\mathrm{H_2}} = 4/2 = 2\ \mathrm{mol}$ and $n_{\mathrm{He}} = 4/4 = 1\ \mathrm{mol}$.

For $P_{\mathrm{Ne}} = P_{\mathrm{He}}$, the mole fractions must match, so $n_{\mathrm{Ne}} = n_{\mathrm{He}} = 1\ \mathrm{mol}$.

With $M_{\mathrm{Ne}} = 20\ \mathrm{g/mol}$, the required mass is $1 \times 20 = 20\ \mathrm{g}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{20\ \mathrm{g}}$

59888.text: In a particular reaction, 4 kJ heat is released by the system and 12 kJ work done on the system. Calculate the $\Delta H$ and $\Delta U$.
59888.sol:
Heat released by the system, $q = -4$ kJ.

Work done on the system, $w = +12$ kJ.

According to the first law of thermodynamics:

$\Delta U = q + w$

$\Delta U = -4 + 12 = 8$ kJ.

For a reaction at constant pressure, the enthalpy change is equal to the heat exchanged:

$\Delta H = q_p = -4$ kJ.

Answer: $\Delta H = -4$ kJ and $\Delta U = 8$ kJ

59910.subject: Chemistry
59910.text: In a reversible expansion, one mole of gas is expanded isothermally at 200 K till its volume increases 10 times. Calculate $\Delta S_{\text{total }}$ at equilibrium?
59910.sol:
For a reversible process, the total entropy change $\Delta S_{\text{total}}$ is defined as $\Delta S_{\text{system}} + \Delta S_{\text{surroundings}}$.

During a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the entropy change of the system is $\Delta S_{\text{system}} = nR \ln \left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right). The surrounding's entropy change is \Delta$ S_{$\text{surroundings}$} = -$\frac{q_{\text{rev}}}{T}, equal to $-$\Delta$ S_{$\text{system}$}$. Consequently, the sum is \Delta$ S_{$\text{total}$} = $\Delta$ S_{$\text{system}$} + (-$\Delta$ S_{$\text{system}$}) = 0$.

Given that $n = 1$ mol, $T = 200$ K, and \frac{V_2}{V_1} =10$, the system's entropy change is \Delta$ S_{\text{system}$} = 8.314 $\cdot \ln(10) $\approx$19.14 \text{ J K}^{-1} and \Delta$ S_{$\text{surroundings}$} $\approx -19.14 \text{ J K}^{-1}, confirming the net effect.

$\boxed{$\text{Zero J}$}$

61676.sol:
Let $u = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{1+x^2} - 1}{x}\right)$ and $v = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)$.

Substituting $x = \tan \theta$, we get:

$u = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{1+\tan^2\theta} - 1}{\tan\theta}\right)$

$u = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sec\theta - 1}{\tan\theta}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\right)$

$u = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2\sin^2(\theta/2)}{2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}x$

Now, for $v$:

$v = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}\right) = \sin^{-1}(\sin 2\theta) = 2\theta = 2\tan^{-1}x$

Differentiating $u$ and $v$ with respect to $x$:

$\dfrac{du}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{2(1+x^2)}$

$\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{2}{1+x^2}$

The derivative of $u$ with respect to $v$ is given by:

$\dfrac{du}{dv} = \dfrac{\dfrac{du}{dx}}{\dfrac{dv}{dx}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2(1+x^2)}}{\dfrac{2}{1+x^2}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{4}$

62001.text: Let $f(x) = ax + b$ and $g(x) = cx + d$. The condition $f(g(x)) = g(f(x))$ holds for all $x$ if and only if...
62001.sol:
Given $f(x) = ax + b$ and $g(x) = cx + d$.

Substituting $g(x)$ into $f(x)$:

$f(g(x)) = a(cx + d) + b = acx + ad + b$

Substituting $f(x)$ into $g(x)$:

$g(f(x)) = c(ax + b) + d = acx + cb + d$

For $f(g(x)) = g(f(x))$ to hold for all $x$, the corresponding coefficients and constant terms must be equal:

$acx + ad + b = acx + cb + d$

$ad + b = cb + d$

Now, evaluating $f(d)$ and $g(b)$:

$f(d) = ad + b$

$g(b) = cb + d$

Therefore, the required condition is $f(d) = g(b)$.

Answer: $f(d) = g(b)$

63351.text: The joint equation of pair of lines through the origin and making an angle of $\frac{\pi}{6}$ with the line $3 x+y-6=0$ is
63351.sol:
The slope of the line $3 x+y-6=0$ is $m_1=-3$. Let $m$ be the slope of one of the lines making an angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$ with $3 x+y-6=0$. $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad \tan \frac{\pi}{6}=\left|\frac{\mathrm{m}-\mathrm{m}_1}{1+\mathrm{m}_1}\right| \\ & \quad \Rightarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\left|\frac{\mathrm{m}-(-3)}{1+\mathrm{m}(-3)}\right| \\ & \quad \Rightarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\left|\frac{\mathrm{m}+3}{1-3 \mathrm{ m}}\right| \end{aligned}$
Squaring on both sides, we get $\begin{aligned} & (1-3 m)^2=3(m+3)^2 \\ & \Rightarrow 6 m^2-24 m-26=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 3 m^2-12 m-13=0 \end{aligned}$
This is the auxiliary equation of two lines and their joint equation is obtained by putting $\mathrm{m}=\frac{y}{x}$. $\therefore \quad$ The joint equation of the lines is $\begin{aligned} & 3\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2-12\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)-13=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 13 x^2+12 x y-3 y^2=0 \end{aligned}$

63944.text: The angles of $\triangle ABC$ are in A.P. and $b : c = \sqrt{3} : \sqrt{2}$ then $\angle A =$
63944.sol:
Given angles $A, B, C$ are in A.P.

$2B = A + C$

Since $A + B + C = 180^{}^{\circ}$, we have $3B = 180^{}^{\circ} \Rightarrow B = 60^{}^{\circ}$

Using the sine rule, $\dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}$

Substituting the given ratio $\dfrac{b}{c} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $B = 60^{}^{\circ}$:

$\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sin 60^{}^{\circ}}{\sin C}$

$\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{\sin C}$

$\sin C = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

Since $B = 60^{}^{\circ}$, $C$ cannot be $135^{}^{\circ}$ (as $B + C = 195^{}^{\circ} > 180^{}^{\circ}$), so $C = 45^{}^{\circ}$

The sum of angles in a triangle is $180^{}^{\circ}$:

$A + B + C = 180^{}^{\circ}$

$A + 60^{}^{\circ} + 45^{}^{\circ} = 180^{}^{\circ}$

$A = 75^{}^{\circ}$

Answer: $75^{}^{\circ}$

64424.subject: Mathematics
64424.text: The unit vectors perpendicular to the plane determined by the points $\mathrm{A}(1,-1,2) \mathrm{ B}(2,0,-1) \mathrm{ C}(0,2,1)$ is
64424.sol:
Perpendicular unit vectors to the plane determined by points $A(1,-1,2)$, $B(2,0,-1)$, and $C(0,2,1)$ can be found by computing the cross product of two vectors in the plane.

The vectors $\vec{AB} = (2-1)\hat{i} + (0-(-1))\hat{j} + (-1-2)\hat{k} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{AC} = (0-1)\hat{i} + (2-(-1))\hat{j} + (1-2)\hat{k} = -\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ lie in the plane.

The cross product $\vec{N} = \vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$ yields a vector perpendicular to the plane:

$\vec{N} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} \text{ and } \hat{j} \text{ and } \hat{k} \\ 1 \text{ and } 1 \text{ and } -3 \\ -1 \text{ and } 3 \text{ and } -1 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(1 \cdot (-1) - (-3) \cdot 3) - \hat{j}(1 \cdot (-1) - (-3) \cdot (-1)) + \hat{k}(1 \cdot 3 - 1 \cdot (-1))$

$\vec{N} = \hat{i}(-1 + 9) - \hat{j}(-1 - 3) + \hat{k}(3 + 1) = 8\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$

The magnitude is $|\vec{N}| = \sqrt{8^2 + 4^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{96} = 4\sqrt{6}$.

The unit vectors are $\pm \frac{\vec{N}}{|\vec{N}|} = \pm \frac{8\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}}{4\sqrt{6}} = \pm \frac{4(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})}{4\sqrt{6}} = \pm \frac{2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}}{\sqrt{6}}$.

This corresponds to option C.

Among the options, only C satisfies this condition.

67295.text:
A body weights 500 Non the surface of earth. At what distance below the surface of earth it weight $250 \mathrm{ N}$ ?
(Radius of earth, $R=6400 \mathrm{ km}$ )
67295.sol:
Value of acceleration due to gravity decreases on going below the surface of the earth. Weight $(w)$ of a body is defined as product of mass $(m)$ and acceleration due to gravity $w=m g$.
The value of g below the surface of earth at a distance $h$ is given by,
$\begin{aligned} & g^{\prime}=g\left(1-\frac{h}{R}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow W^{\prime}=W\left(1-\frac{h}{R}\right)\end{aligned}$
Given, $W^{\prime}=250 \mathrm{~N}$ and $W=500\begin{aligned} & 250=500\left(1-\frac{h}{R}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow h=\frac{R}{2}=32000 \mathrm{~km}\end{aligned}$

Surface Energy Transformation of Liquid Droplets

Let $R$ be the radius of the original liquid drop, with surface area $A_1 = 4\pi R^2$ and initial surface energy $E = \sigma A_1$, where $\sigma$ is the surface tension.

The drop is divided into 729 smaller droplets of equal size. By conservation of volume, the total volume remains unchanged.

Volume of original drop: $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3$
Volume of one small droplet: $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$
Equating total volumes: $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 729 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$
Simplifying: $R^3 = 729r^3 \Rightarrow R = 9r \Rightarrow r = \frac{R}{9}$

The surface area of one small droplet is $a = 4\pi r^2$.
Total final surface area: $A_2 = 729 \times 4\pi r^2 = 729 \times 4\pi \left(\frac{R}{9}\right)^2 = \frac{729}{81} \times 4\pi R^2 = 9 \times 4\pi R^2$

Final surface energy: $E_{\text{final}} = \sigma A_2 = \sigma (9 \times 4\pi R^2) = 9E$

Thus, the surface energy increases by a factor of 9.

$\boxed{9E}$

70130.text:
In biprism experiment, the maximum intensity is $I_0$. If the path difference between the two interfering waves is $\dfrac{\lambda}{3}$, then intensity at the point on the screen is
[$\sin 30^{}^{\circ} = \cos 60^{}^{\circ} = 0.5$, $\sin 60^{}^{\circ} = \cos 30^{}^{\circ} = \sqrt{3}/2$]
70130.sol:
The phase difference $\phi$ is related to the path difference $\Delta x$ by the relation:

$\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x$

Given $\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{3}$, the phase difference is:

$\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \dfrac{\lambda}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$

The intensity $I$ at a point on the screen is given by:

$I = I_0 \cos^2 \left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)

Substituting the value of $\phi$:

$I = I_0 \cos^2 $\left(\dfrac{2\pi/3}{2}\right) = I_0 \cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$

Since $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \cos 60^{}^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, we get:

$I = I_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{I_0}{4}$

Minimum resolvable separation is determined using Rayleigh's criterion, where the angular resolution $\theta = \frac{1.22\lambda}{a}$ depends on the wavelength $\lambda = 500 \text{ nm}$ and aperture diameter $a = 0.5 \text{ cm}$.

The pupil diameter $a = 0.5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$ and $\lambda = 500 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$ yield $\theta = \frac{1.22 \times (500 \times 10^{-9})}{0.5 \times 10^{-2}} = 1.22 \times 10^{-4} \text{ radians}$.

At viewing distance $D = 0.25 \text{ m}$, the linear separation is $x = D\theta = 0.25 \times (1.22 \times 10^{-4}) = 3.05 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}$.

Converting to micrometers: $x = 30.5 \mu\text{m}$, which corresponds to option B.

71574.text: Stomatal transpiration takes place during day time in the following plants EXCEPT________.
71574.sol:
Cactus is a xerophytic plant that exhibits Crassulacean Acid Metabolism (CAM).

In CAM plants, the stomata remain closed during the daytime to prevent excessive water loss through transpiration.

The stomata open during the night (scotoactive stomata) to take in carbon dioxide.

Therefore, stomatal transpiration does not take place during the daytime in Cactus, whereas it occurs during the daytime in Lotus, Mango, and Grass.

Answer: Cactus

71988.subject: Chemistry
71988.text:
0.636 g of acetic acid (molar mass = 60 g/mol) is dissolved in 1 kg of water, the solution freezes at $-0.0205^{}^{\circ}$ C.
Calculate van't Hoff factor of acetic acid ($\text{K}_f$ water = 1.86 K-kg/mol)
71988.sol:
Given:
Mass of acetic acid, $w = 0.636$ g
Molar mass of acetic acid, $M = 60$ g/mol
Mass of solvent (water), $W = 1$ kg
Depression in freezing point, $\Delta T_f = 0 - (-0.0205) = 0.0205$ K
Cryoscopic constant, $K_f = 1.86$ K kg/mol

The molality ($m$) of the solution is calculated as:
$m = \dfrac{w}{M \times W} = \dfrac{0.636}{60 \times 1} = 0.0106$ mol/kg

Using the formula for depression in freezing point:
$\Delta T_f = i \times K_f \times m$

Substituting the given values:
$0.0205 = i \times 1.86 \times 0.0106$

$0.0205 = i \times 0.019716$

$i = \dfrac{0.0205}{0.019716} \approx 1.041$

Answer: $1.041$

72172.subject: Physics
72172.text: The self inductance L of a solenoid of length $l$ and area of cross-section A, with a fixed number of turns N increases as
72172.sol:
The self-inductance of a long solenoid is given by the formula:

$L = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l}$

where $N$ is the total number of turns, $A$ is the cross-sectional area, and $l$ is the length of the solenoid.

Since the number of turns $N$ is fixed, the self-inductance $L$ is directly proportional to the area of cross-section $A$ and inversely proportional to the length $l$.

$L \propto \dfrac{A}{l}$

Thus, to increase the self-inductance $L$, the area $A$ must increase and the length $l$ must decrease.

Answer: $l$ decreases and A increases.

72445.subject: Physics
72445.text: In the Young's double slit experiment, the intensity of light at a point on the screen is 'K', $\lambda$ being the wavelength of light used. The intensity at a point where path difference is $\dfrac{\lambda}{6}$ will be $\left[\cos \left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right]$
72445.sol:
The maximum intensity in Young's double slit experiment is given as $I_{max} = K$.

The phase difference $\phi$ is related to the path difference $\Delta x$ by the formula:

$\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x$

Given the path difference $\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{6}$, the phase difference is:

$\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \dfrac{\lambda}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$

The intensity $I$ at any point on the screen is given by:

$I = I_{max} \cos^2\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)$

Substituting the values of $I_{max}$ and $\phi$:

$I = K \cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$

Since $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, we get:

$I = K \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{3K}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3K}{4}$

72482.subject: Physics
72482.text: The density of oxygen is 16 times that of hydrogen. The ratio of the velocity of sound in oxygen to that in hydrogen is
72482.sol:
The velocity of sound in a gas is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma P}{\rho}}$.

For oxygen and hydrogen, both being diatomic gases, the ratio of specific heats $\gamma$ is the same. Assuming they are at the same pressure $P$, the velocity of sound is inversely proportional to the square root of the density of the gas.

$v \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\rho}}$

$\dfrac{v_{O}}{v_{H}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\rho_{H}}{\rho_{O}}}$

Given $\rho_{O} = 16 \rho_{H}$,

$\dfrac{v_{O}}{v_{H}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\rho_{H}}{16 \rho_{H}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{16}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

The ratio of the velocity of sound in oxygen to that in hydrogen is $1:4$.

Answer: $1:4$

Madurai, located in Tamil Nadu, while predominantly known for the Meenakshi Amman Temple (a Hindu site), also has significant historical connections to Jainism. There are several Jain caves and rock beds containing ancient inscriptions and carvings of Tirthankaras in the hills surrounding Madurai, such as Samanar Hills, indicating it was an important Jain center in antiquity.

Sonagiri, located in Madhya Pradesh, is a highly revered Digambara Jain pilgrimage site, known for its numerous white temples scattered across the hills, marking the place where many ascetics achieved salvation.

Therefore, all three towns are associated with significant Jain pilgrimage or historical sites.

77999.subject: Mathematics
77999.text: If two fair dice are tossed, then what is the probability that the sum of the numbers on the faces of the dice is strictly greater than 7?
77999.sol:
Total number of possible outcomes when two fair dice are tossed is $6 \times 6 = 36$.

Let $S$ be the sum of the numbers on the faces of the dice. By symmetry, the probability of getting a sum strictly greater than $7$ is equal to the probability of getting a sum strictly less than $7$.

$P(S > 7) + P(S < 7) + P(S = 7) = 1$

The outcomes for $S = 7$ are $(1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1)$, which are $6$ in number. Thus, $P(S = 7) = \dfrac{6}{36} = \dfrac{1}{6}$.

$2 P(S > 7) + \dfrac{1}{6} = 1$

$2 P(S > 7) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{5}{6}$

$P(S > 7) = \dfrac{5}{12}$

79247.text: Let $\theta$ be the angle between two unit vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$. If $\vec{a}+2 \vec{b}$ is perpendicular to $5 \vec{a}-4 \vec{b}$, then what is $\cos \theta+\cos 2 \theta$ equal to?
79247.sol:
Since, $(\vec{a}+2 \vec{b}) \ \text{$ and $} (5 \vec{a}-4 \vec{b})$ are perpendicular vectors.
$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow(\vec{a}+2 \vec{b}) \cdot(5 \vec{a}-4 \vec{b})=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 5|\vec{a}|^2-4 \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+10 \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}-8|\vec{b}|^2=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 5 \times 1+6 \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}-8=0 \quad \text{ Since, }|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|=1 \\
& \Rightarrow 6|\vec{a}||\vec{b}| \cos \theta=3 \\
& \Rightarrow 1 \cdot 1 \cos \theta=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \cos \theta=\frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}$
So, $\cos 2 \theta=2 \cos ^2 \theta-1=2 \times \frac{1}{4}-1=-\frac{1}{2}$
Now, $\cos \theta+\cos 2 \theta=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}=0$

82658.subject: Physics
82658.text:
Consider a fixed uniformly charged insulating sphere with radius $R$ and total charge $+Q$. A point charge $-q$ ($q\ll Q$) with mass $m$ is released from rest at a distance of $3R$ from the centre of the charged sphere. When the point charge reaches the surface of the sphere, its speed is :
($\epsilon_0$ is the permittivity of vacuum, neglect gravitational forces).
82658.sol:
Initial potential energy of the system when the charge $-q$ is at a distance of $3R$ from the centre is:

$U_i = -\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{Qq}{3R}$

Final potential energy of the system when the charge reaches the surface of the sphere (distance $R$ from the centre) is:

$U_f = -\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{Qq}{R}$

According to the principle of conservation of mechanical energy:

$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$

$0 - \dfrac{Qq}{12\pi\epsilon_0 R} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R}$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R} - \dfrac{Qq}{12\pi\epsilon_0 R}$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R} \left( 1 - \dfrac{1}{3} \right)$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{2Qq}{12\pi\epsilon_0 R}$

$v^2 = \dfrac{Qq}{3\pi\epsilon_0 mR}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{Qq}{3\pi\epsilon_0 mR}}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{Qq}{3\pi\epsilon_0 mR}}$

84043.text: The WBC count of a person's blood sample is $8000$/cu.mm. How many eosinophils and lymphocytes would be in the same blood sample approximately ?

Total WBC count = $8000$/cu.mm.

Eosinophils constitute $2 - 3\%$ of total WBCs.

Lymphocytes constitute $20 - 25\%$ of total WBCs.

Number of lymphocytes = $\dfrac{20}{100} \times 8000$ to $\dfrac{25}{100} \times 8000 = 1600 - 2000$/cu.mm.

84114.subject: Zoology
84114.text: If you suspect major deficiency of antibodies in a person, to which of the following would you look for confirmatory evidence?
84114.sol:
Chemically, antibodies are globular proteins, belong to a class of serum proteins, which are called $\gamma$ or gamma globulins. Thus, the antibodies are also known as immunoglobulins and are produced by the lymphocytes. Hence, to confirm the deficiency of antibodies in a person, serum globulins will be tested.
Related Theory
Blood proteins, also termed plasma proteins, are proteins present in blood plasma. 90-92 per cent of plasma is water and proteins contribute 6-8 per cent of it. Fibrinogen, globulins and albumins are the major proteins. Fibrinogens are needed for clotting or coagulation of blood. Globulins primarily are involved in defense mechanisms of the body and the albumins help in osmotic balance.

85152.subject: Zoology
85152.text: Under which condition the gene ratio remains constant for any species?
85152.sol:
Genetic equilibrium means that the frequency of occurrence of alleles of a gene is supposed to remain fixed and even remain the same through generations. Gene frequencies tend to remain constant from generation to generation when disturbing factors are not present. Factors that disturb the natural equilibrium of gene frequencies include mutation, migration (or gene flow), random genetic drift, and natural selection.
Related Theory
Random mating involves the mating of individuals regardless of any physical, genetic or social preference. In other words, the mating between two organisms is not influenced by any environmental, hereditary or social interaction. Hence, potential mates have an equal chance of being selected.

${cos}^{2}x = {tan}^{2}y = {sec}^{2}y - 1 = {cot}^{2}z - 1$

$⇒ \left(2 - {sin}^{2}x\right)\left(1 - 2{sin}^{2}x\right) = {sin}^{2}x$
$⇒ 2{sin}^{4}x - 6{sin}^{2}x + 2 = 0$
$⇒ {sin}^{2}x = \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{9 - 4}}{2} = \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$
but ${sin}^{2}x \in \left[0, 1\right]$ so rejecting ${sin}^{2}x = \dfrac{3 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$
we have, ${sin}^{2}x = \dfrac{3 - \sqrt{5}}{2} = {\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}\right)}^{2}$
$⇒ sin ⁡ x = \dfrac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2} ⇒ 2sin ⁡ \theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}$
$⇒ sin ⁡ \theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{4} ⇒ \theta = {18}^{o}$

94624.subject: Physics
94624.text: An ideal monatomic gas is confined in a cylinder by a spring-loaded massless piston of cross-section $8 \times {10}^{- 3}m^{2}$. The piston can slide on the walls of the cylinder without any friction. Initially, the gas is at $300K$ and occupies a volume of $2.4 \times {10}^{- 3}m^{3}$ and the spring is in its relaxed position. Now, gas is slowly heated by a small electric heater and the piston moves out slowly by $0.1 m$. Calculate the final temperature of the gas and the heat supplied by the heater. The force constant of the spring is $8000N / m$ and atmospheric pressure is $1 \times {10}^{5}N / m^{2}$.
94624.sol:
In the initial condition

${P}_{1} = {10}^{5}Pa$, ${V}_{1} = 2 . 4 \times {10}^{- 3}m^{3}$, ${T}_{1} = 300K$

Finally,

${P}_{2} = {P}_{1} + \dfrac{kx}{A} = 2 \times {10}^{5}Pa$

${V}_{2} = {V}_{1} + Ax = 3 . 2 \times {10}^{- 3}m^{3}$

$\dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}}{T1} = \dfrac{{P}_{2}{V}_{2}}{T2}$, on solving we get

${T}_{2} = 800K$

Applying work-energy theorem for the piston

${W}_{gas} + {W}_{atmos} + {W}_{spring} = 0$

${W}_{gas} = {P}_{0}Ax + \dfrac{1}{2}kx^{2} = 120J$

$\Delta U = n{C}_{V} \Delta T = nR \Delta T\left(\gamma - 1\right) = {P}_{2}{V}_{2} - {P}_{1}{V}_{1}\left(\gamma - 1\right) = 600J$

$Q = \Delta U + {W}_{gas} = 600 + 120 = 720J$

95286.subject: Botany
95286.text: Which one of the following is NOT a characteristic of meristematic cells?
95286.sol: The cells residing at the root and shoot tips are known as meristem cells. These are undifferentiated cells and are responsible for the plant growth due to its ability to divide. These cells are small and have thin cellulosic cell walls with large nuclei, small or absent vacuoles, and absence of intercellular spaces. These cells also help to increase the length of the plant as well as the girth (lateral growth) of the stem, branches and roots.

98299.subject: Chemistry
98299.text: Which of the following is a co-factor for the proteolytic enzyme carboxypeptidase?
98299.sol: Enzymes are proteinaceous in nature. Some enzymes also contain non-protein part known as co-factors. These factors are attached to the enzyme to enhanced their catalytic activity. The protein part of the enzyme is known as apoenzyme. Hence, apoenzyme (protein part) + Co-factors (non-protein part) = holoenzyme (whole enzyme).As the co-factors are bound to enzymes, the removal of these factors affects the overall activity of enzymes too. These co-factors can be organic or inorganic. Organic cofactors if tightly bound are known as prosthetic groups and if loosely bound are termed as co-enzymes. The inorganic co-factors are metal ions. Example of inorganic co-factor is zinc which is a co-factor of enzyme carboxypeptidase.

The velocity of the chemical reaction at which the substrate concentration is half its maximum value
98465.sol: Km (Michaelis Menten Constant) is the substrate concentration at which the chemical reaction attains half of its maximum velocity. With the increase in concentration of substrate, the enzymatic velocity also increases. At a certain value all the active site of the enzyme molecules are saturated. Increase in substrate concentration does not increase the velocity of the enzymatic reaction. Higher is the affinity of an enzyme for a substrate, lower is the Km value. Km value lies in between ${10}^{- 1}$ to ${10}^{- 6}M$. Km value is independent of enzyme and substrate concentration.

102412.subject: Physics
102412.text: A simple pendulum is suspended from the ceiling of a stationary truck, and its time period of small oscillations is $T$. If the truck suddenly starts accelerating horizontally with an acceleration of $\sqrt{3}g$, the new time period of the pendulum becomes $T'$. The ratio $\dfrac{T'}{T}$ is:
102412.sol:
When the truck is stationary, the time period of the simple pendulum is given by:
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$

When the truck accelerates horizontally with acceleration $a = \sqrt{3}g$, the pendulum is in a non-inertial frame. The effective acceleration due to gravity $g_{\text{eff}}$ is the vector sum of the actual gravity $g$ downwards and the pseudo acceleration $a$ horizontally.

$g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{g^2 + a^2}$
$g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{g^2 + (\sqrt{3}g)^2} = \sqrt{g^2 + 3g^2} = \sqrt{4g^2} = 2g$

The new time period $T'$ of the pendulum in the accelerating truck is:
$T' = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g_{\text{eff}}}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{2g}}$

Taking the ratio of the new time period to the original time period:
$\dfrac{T'}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{2g}}}{2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

102734.subject: Physics
102734.text: A closed organ pipe of length 20 cm is sounded with tuning fork in resonance. What is the frequency of tuning fork? $(v=332 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s})$
102734.sol: Key Idea : When length of air column is $\frac{\lambda}{4}$, then first resonance occurs. If we adjust the length of air-column in closed organ pipe as such its any natural frequency equals to the frequency of tuning fork, then the amplitude of forced vibrations of air-column increases very much. This is the state of resonance. At first resonance $l=\frac{\lambda}{4}$ So, frequency of tuning fork $f=\frac{v}{\lambda}=\frac{v}{4 l}$ Given, $l=20 \mathrm{~cm}=0.2 \mathrm{~m}, v=332 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ Hence, $f=\frac{332}{4 \times 0.2}=415 \mathrm{~Hz}$

103290.subject: Physics
103290.text:
A uniform wire AB of resistance $R_0$ is connected across an ideal DC voltage source $V_0$. A resistor $R$ is connected between end A and a sliding contact C on the wire. Let $x$ be the fractional distance of C from A (where $x = \text{AC}/\text{AB}$). Based on this circuit, two statements are given below:

Statement I: As the sliding contact moves from A to B, the potential difference across $R$ increases monotonically.
Statement II: If $R \gg R_0$, the potential difference across $R$ varies approximately linearly with $x$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
103290.sol:
The resistance of segment AC is $x R_0$ and segment CB is $(1-x) R_0$.

The equivalent resistance of AC and $R$ in parallel is $R_p = \dfrac{R (x R_0)}{R + x R_0}$.

The total resistance of the circuit is $R_{eq} = R_p + (1-x) R_0 = \dfrac{R x R_0}{R + x R_0} + (1-x) R_0 = \dfrac{R R_0 + x R_0^2 - x^2 R_0^2}{R + x R_0}$.

The potential difference across $R$ is $V(x) = V_0 \dfrac{R_p}{R_{eq}} = V_0 \dfrac{R x}{R + x(1-x)R_0}$.

To check Statement I, we can write $\dfrac{V_0}{V(x)} = \dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{(1-x)R_0}{R}$. As $x$ increases from $0$ to $1$, both $\dfrac{1}{x}$ and $(1-x)$ strictly decrease, so $\dfrac{V_0}{V(x)}$ decreases. This means $V(x)$ increases monotonically. Statement I is correct.

For Statement II, if $R \gg R_0$, the term $x(1-x)R_0$ in the denominator can be neglected compared to $R$. Thus, $V(x) \approx V_0 \dfrac{R x}{R} = V_0 x$. This shows a linear relationship with $x$. Statement II is correct.

Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

103925.subject: Physics
103925.text: Two pairs of concentric circular coils are placed in the same plane. Pair A consists of an inner coil of radius $r$ and an outer coil of radius $R$ (where $R \gg r$). Pair B consists of an inner coil of radius $2r$ and an outer coil of radius $2R$. A time-varying current $I(t)$ with a constant rate of change flows in the outer coils of both pairs. What is the ratio of the induced emf in the inner coil of Pair A to that of Pair B?
103925.sol:
The induced emf in the inner coil is given by $E = M \dfrac{dI}{dt}$, where $M$ is the mutual inductance between the outer and inner coils.

The magnetic field at the centre due to the outer coil is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.
The flux linked with the inner coil is $\Phi = B \times \pi r^2 = \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\right) \pi r^2$.
Thus, the mutual inductance is $M = \dfrac{\Phi}{I} = \dfrac{\mu_0 \pi r^2}{2R}$.

For Pair A, the mutual inductance is:
$M_A = \dfrac{\mu_0 \pi r^2}{2R}$

For Pair B, the inner radius is $2r$ and the outer radius is $2R$. The mutual inductance is:
$M_B = \dfrac{\mu_0 \pi (2r)^2}{2(2R)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 \pi (4r^2)}{4R} = \dfrac{\mu_0 \pi r^2}{R}$

Comparing $M_A$ and $M_B$, we see that $M_B = 2 M_A$.

Since the rate of change of current $\dfrac{dI}{dt}$ is the same for both pairs, the ratio of the induced emfs is simply the ratio of their mutual inductances:
$\dfrac{E_A}{E_B} = \dfrac{M_A}{M_B} = \dfrac{M_A}{2M_A} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Answer: $1/2$

105891.subject: Chemistry
105891.text:
The number of carbon atoms present in $18$ g of glucose is :
(Given : $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}$ particles mol$^{-1}$)
105891.sol:
The chemical formula of glucose is $C_6H_{12}O_6$.

Molar mass of glucose $= (6 \times 12) + (12 \times 1) + (6 \times 16) = 180$ g mol$^{-1}$.

Number of moles of glucose $= \dfrac{18}{180} = 0.1$ mol.

One molecule of glucose contains $6$ carbon atoms.

Number of moles of carbon atoms $= 6 \times 0.1 = 0.6$ mol.

Total number of carbon atoms $= 0.6 \times N_A = 0.6 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.6132 \times 10^{23} \approx 3.613 \times 10^{23}$.

Answer: $3.613 \times 10^{23}$

119890.subject: Chemistry
119890.text:
Consider the following sequence of reactions:

$\text{Nitrobenzene} \xrightarrow{\text{Sn} / \text{HCl}} \text{A} \xrightarrow[\text{273-278 K}]{\text{NaNO}_2 / \text{HCl}} \text{B} \xrightarrow{\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}} \text{C}$

The major product $\text{C}$ is:
119890.sol:
Nitrobenzene is reduced by $\text{Sn} / \text{HCl}$ to form aniline ($\text{A}$).

Aniline undergoes diazotization with $\text{NaNO}_2$ and $\text{HCl}$ at $\text{273-278 K}$ to form benzenediazonium chloride ($\text{B}$).

Benzenediazonium chloride is treated with ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), which acts as a mild reducing agent. It reduces the diazonium salt to benzene ($\text{C}$) while being oxidized to ethanal.

Therefore, the major product $\text{C}$ is benzene. Ethoxybenzene is incorrect as ethanol acts as a reducing agent, not a nucleophile. Phenol would be formed if the diazonium salt was warmed with water. Chlorobenzene would be formed in a Sandmeyer or Gattermann reaction.

Answer: $\text{Benzene}$

121025.subject: Chemistry
121025.text: Oral contraceptive pills containing estrogen and progesterone are highly effective when taken orally, whereas insulin for diabetes management must be administered via injection. What is the primary biochemical basis for this difference in the route of administration?
options: Insulin is a steroid hormone that is poorly absorbed, while oral contraceptives are easily absorbed proteins.
Insulin is rapidly excreted by the kidneys if taken orally, whereas oral contraceptives are retained in the blood.
Oral contraceptives elicit a weaker immune response in the gut compared to oral insulin.
Insulin is a peptide hormone susceptible to digestion by gastrointestinal proteases, whereas oral contraceptives are steroid hormones.
121025.sol:
Estrogen and progesterone present in oral contraceptive pills are steroid hormones (lipid-derived) and are not degraded by proteolytic enzymes in the gastrointestinal tract.

In contrast, insulin is a peptide hormone. If taken orally, the peptide bonds of insulin would be broken down (digested) by proteases in the stomach and intestine, rendering it biologically inactive before it can be absorbed into the bloodstream. Therefore, it must be injected.

Answer: Insulin is a peptide hormone susceptible to digestion by gastrointestinal proteases, whereas oral contraceptives are steroid hormones.

122047.subject: Botany
122047.text:
Consider the following components of vascular tissues:
(a) Tracheids
(b) Vessels
(c) Sieve cells
(d) Sieve tube elements
(e) Companion cells
(f) Albuminous cells

How many of the above structures are normally present in the complex tissues of a typical gymnosperm?
122047.sol:
In gymnosperms, the xylem consists mainly of tracheids, while vessels are generally absent. The phloem of gymnosperms contains sieve cells and albuminous cells, but lacks sieve tube elements and companion cells.

Evaluating the given list:
(a) Tracheids - Present
(b) Vessels - Absent
(c) Sieve cells - Present
(d) Sieve tube elements - Absent
(e) Companion cells - Absent
(f) Albuminous cells - Present

Thus, exactly three of the listed structures are present in the complex tissues of a typical gymnosperm.

Answer: Three

124751.subject: Botany
124751.text:
Match the phases of plant growth in List-I with their corresponding cellular characteristics in List-II.

List-IList-II
A. Meristematic phase1. Maximal wall thickening
B. Elongation phase2. Abundant plasmodesmatal connections
C. Maturation phase3. Increased vacuolation
4. Dedifferentiation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
124751.sol:
The period of growth is divided into three phases: meristematic, elongation, and maturation.

Meristematic phase (A) cells are rich in protoplasm, possess large conspicuous nuclei, and have thin primary cellulosic cell walls with abundant plasmodesmatal connections (2).

Elongation phase (B) cells are characterised by increased vacuolation (3), cell enlargement, and new cell wall deposition.

Maturation phase (C) cells attain their maximal size in terms of wall thickening (1) and protoplasmic modifications.

Dedifferentiation (4) is a separate phenomenon where differentiated cells regain the capacity to divide, not a characteristic of the primary growth phases.

Therefore, the correct match is A-2, B-3, C-1.

Answer: A-2, B-3, C-1

124915.subject: Botany
124915.text: What is the energy released during oxidation in respiration used to synthesize?
124915.sol: During oxidation within a cell, all the energy contained in respiratory substrates is not released free into the cell, or in a single step. It is released in a series of slow stepwise reactions controlled by enzymes, and it is trapped as chemical energy in the form of ATP. Hence, it is important to understand that the energy released by oxidation in respiration is not (or rather cannot be) used directly but is used to synthesize ATP, which is broken down whenever (and wherever) energy needs to be utilized. Hence, ATP acts as the energy currency of the cell. This energy trapped in ATP is utilized in various energy-requiring processes of the organisms, and the carbon skeleton produced during respiration is used as precursors for biosynthesis of other molecules in the cell.
124915.meta: What is the energy released during oxidation in respiration used to synthesize?

125325.subject: Botany
125325.text: What organisms did Cornelius van Niel study to demonstrate photosynthesis?
125325.sol: A milestone contribution to the understanding of photosynthesis was that made by a microbiologist, Cornelius van Niel (1897-1985), who, based on his studies of purple and green bacteria, demonstrated that photosynthesis is essentially a light-dependent reaction in which hydrogen from a suitable oxidisable compound reduces carbon dioxide to carbohydrates. In green plants H2O is the hydrogen donor and is oxidised to O2 . Some organisms do not release O2 during photosynthesis. When H2 S, instead is the hydrogen donor for purple and green sulphur bacteria, the ‘oxidation’ product is sulphur or sulphate depending on the organism and not O2 . Hence, he inferred that the O2 evolved by the green plant comes from H2O, not from carbon dioxide.
125325.meta: What organisms did Cornelius van Niel study to demonstrate photosynthesis?

125330.subject: Botany
125330.text: How do chloroplasts usually align themselves in mesophyll cells?
options: Along the walls of the cells
In the center of the cells
At the bottom of the cells
125330.sol: The mesophyll cells in the leaves have a large number of chloroplasts. Usually the chloroplasts align themselves along the walls of the mesophyll cells, such that they get the optimum quantity of the incident light. Within the chloroplast there is membranous system consisting of grana, the stroma lamellae, and the matrix stroma (Figure 11.2). There is a clear division of labour within the chloroplast. The membrane system is responsible for trapping the light energy and also for the synthesis of ATP and NADPH. In stroma, enzymatic reactions synthesise sugar, which in turn forms starch. The former set of reactions, since they are directly light driven are called light reactions (photochemical reactions). The latter are not directly light driven but are dependent on the products of light reactions (ATP and NADPH). Hence, to distinguish the latter they are called, by convention, as dark reactions (carbon reactions). However, this should not be construed to mean that they occur in darkness or that they are not light-dependent.
125330.meta: How do chloroplasts usually align themselves in mesophyll cells?

125443.subject: Botany
125443.sol: The particularly large cells around the vascular bundles of the C4 plants are called bundle sheath cells, and the leaves which have such anatomy are said to have ‘Kranz’ anatomy. ‘Kranz’ means ‘wreath’ and is a reflection of the arrangement of cells. The bundle sheath cells may form several layers around the vascular bundles; they are characterised by having a large number of chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange and no intercellular spaces. You may like to cut a section of the leaves of C4 plants – maize or sorghum – to observe the Kranz anatomy and the distribution of mesophyll cells.

127213.subject: Botany
127213.text: What is the primary benefit of biodiversity?
127213.sol: The broadly utilitarian argument says that biodiversity plays a major role in many ecosystem services that nature provides. The fast dwindling Amazon forest is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, 20 per cent of the total oxygen in the earth’s atmosphere. Can we put an economic value on this service by nature? You can get some idea by finding out how much your neighborhood hospital spends on a cylinder of oxygen. Pollination (without which plants cannot give us fruits or seeds) is another service, ecosystems provide through pollinators layer – bees, bumblebees, birds and bats. What will be the costs of accomplishing pollination without help from natural pollinators? There are other intangible benefits – that we derive from nature–the aesthetic pleasures of walking through thick woods, watching spring flowers in full bloom or waking up to a bulbul’s song in the morning.

128705.text: Assertion : Emulsification is necessary for the digestion of fats.Reason : After fats are emulsified, the action of enzyme amylase gets signi-ficantly increased.
options: If both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion
If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion
If assertion is true but reason is false
If both assertion and reason are false
128705.sol: Being insoluble in water, fats and oils form large immiscible droplets in aqueous media but the enzymes which hydrolyse fats and oils (called lipases) are insoluble in fats and soluble in water. Therefore, lipases can act only on the water adjoining surfaces of fat droplets. Evidently, the larger the surface area of fat droplets, the greater is the action of the lipase on them. We know that the smaller the size of a droplet, the larger is its surface area relative to its mass. Thus lipases can digest fat in significant amounts only when large fat droplets are broken into tiny droplets to form a fine emulsion. This is the reason why emulsification is so necessary for the digestion of fats. Enzyme amylase, on the other hand, is a starch - hydrolysing enzyme which has no role in fat digestion.

129493.subject: Zoology
129493.text: What is the purpose of Bowman's capsule in the renal tubule?
options: To divide the renal tubule into many parts
129493.sol: The renal tubule begins with a double walled cup-like structure called Bowman’s capsule, which encloses the glomerulus. Glomerulus alongwith Bowman’s capsule, is called the malpighian body or renal corpuscle (Figure 16.4). The tubule continues further to form a highly coiled network – proximal convoluted tubule (PCT). A hairpin shaped Henle’s loop is the next part of the tubule which has a descending and an ascending limb. The ascending limb continues as another highly coiled tubular region called distal convoluted tubule (DCT). The DCTs of many nephrons open into a straight tube called collecting duct, many of which converge and open into the renal pelvis through medullary pyramids in the calyces.

131245.text:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the stages and timing of oogenesis in human females.

List-I (Cell/Event)List-II (Stage/Timing)
A. Oogonia formation1. Prophase-I of Meiosis
B. Primary oocyte arrest2. Embryonic development
C. First polar body formation3. During fertilization
D. Second polar body formation4. Puberty (prior to ovulation)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
131245.sol:
A. Oogonia formation: Oogenesis is initiated during the embryonic development stage when a couple of million oogonia are formed within each fetal ovary. (A matches with 2)

B. Primary oocyte arrest: The oogonia start division and enter into prophase-I of the meiotic division and get temporarily arrested at that stage, called primary oocytes. (B matches with 1)

C. First polar body formation: The primary oocyte within the tertiary follicle grows in size and completes its first meiotic division prior to ovulation (at puberty), forming a large secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body. (C matches with 4)

D. Second polar body formation: The secondary meiotic division is completed only upon the entry of a sperm during fertilization, resulting in the formation of a second polar body and an ovum. (D matches with 3)

Therefore, the correct matching is A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3.

Answer: A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3

131846.subject: Zoology
131846.text: In the lac operon of E. coli, the repressor protein synthesized by the i gene exerts its regulatory effect by:
options: binding to the promoter region to prevent RNA polymerase from attaching.
binding to the operator region to prevent RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes.
binding directly to the structural genes to prevent their translation into enzymes.
binding to the inducer molecule to prevent the initiation of transcription.
131846.sol:
The i gene synthesizes the repressor protein constitutively. This repressor protein binds specifically to the operator region of the operon. This physical binding creates an obstacle that prevents RNA polymerase (which binds to the adjacent promoter) from accessing and transcribing the structural genes.

Option 1 is incorrect because RNA polymerase binds to the promoter, not the repressor. Option 3 is incorrect because the repressor targets the operator, not the structural genes themselves, and it inhibits transcription, not translation. Option 4 is incorrect because when the repressor binds to the inducer, it becomes inactive and allows transcription to proceed, rather than preventing it.

Answer: binding to the operator region to prevent RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes.

132287.subject: Zoology
132287.text: If a man with blood group AB marries a woman with blood group O, what blood groups can be expected in their offspring?
132287.sol:
Refer: NCERT | Class 12 | Page: 61 | Paragraph: 2

The genotype of the man with blood group AB is $I^A I^B$.

The genotype of the woman with blood group O is $i i$.

The gametes produced by the man are $I^A$ and $I^B$.

The gamete produced by the woman is $i$.

Crossing the gametes, the possible genotypes of the offspring are $I^A i$ and $I^B i$.

The genotype $I^A i$ corresponds to blood group A, and the genotype $I^B i$ corresponds to blood group B.

Therefore, the expected blood groups in their offspring are A and B only.

Answer: (2) A and B only

132668.subject: Zoology
132668.text: What did similar experiments to Miller’s reveal?
options: Formation of sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments, and fats
132668.sol: Oparin of Russia and Haldane of England proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (e.g. RNA, protein, etc.) and that formation of life was preceded by chemical evolution, i.e., formation of diverse organic molecules from inorganic constituents. The conditions on earth were – high temperature, volcanic storms, In 1953, S.L. Miller, an American scientist created similar conditions on a laboratory scale. He created electric discharge in a closed flask containing CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 8000C. He observed formation of amino acids. In similar experiments others observed, formation of sugars, nitrogen bases, pigment and fats. Analysis of meteorite content also revealed similar compounds indicating that similar processes are occurring elsewhere in space. With this limited evidence, the first part of the conjectured story, i.e., chemical evolution was more or less accepted. S.L. Miller created conditions similar to early Earth’s atmosphere, including electric discharge, in a laboratory experiment.

132720.subject: Zoology
132720.text: According to Hugo de Vries, how do mutations compare to Darwinian variations?
options: Mutations are small and directional, while Darwinian variations are large and random
Mutations are random and directionless, while Darwinian variations are small and directional
Mutations are gradual, while Darwinian variations are sudden
Both mutations and Darwinian variations are gradual
132720.sol: What is the origin of this variation and how does speciation occur? Even though Mendel had talked of inheritable 'factors' influencing phenotype, Darwin either ignored these observations or kept silence. In the first decade of the twentieth century, Hugo deVries based his work on evening primrose brought forth the idea of mutations – large differences arising suddenly in a population. He believed that it is mutation which causes evolution and not the minor variations (heritable) that Darwin talked about. Mutations are random and directionless while Darwinian variations are small and directional. Evolution for Darwin was gradual while deVries believed mutation caused speciation and hence called it saltation (single step large mutation).Studies in population genetics, later, brought out some clarity.

Genetic variation in a population Arise due to reshuffling of genes caused by recombination and mutations. Reproductive isolation and selection do not cause variation, as due to this, selective genome cause inheritance of similar traits in offspring.
Related Theory
According to Hugo de Vries mutation theory. new species arise suddenly showing abrupt deviations in characters from the normal forms. The mutation theory differs from Darwin's theory in the nature of the variations, whereas continuous variations are the raw materials for the formation of new species in Darwin's theory of natural selection; but in De Vries theory. discontinuous variation or mutations are the raw materials.

134629.sol: Agrobacterium tumifaciens, a pathogen of several dicot plants is able to deliver a piece of DNA known as ‘T-DNA’ to transform normal plant cells into a tumor and direct these tumor cells to produce the chemicals required by the pathogen. Similarly, retroviruses in animals have the ability to transform normal cells into cancerous cells. A better understanding of the art of delivering genes by pathogens in their eukaryotic hosts has generated knowledge to transform these tools of pathogens into useful vectors for delivering genes of interest to humans. The tumor inducing (Ti) plasmid of Agrobacterium tumifaciens has now been modified into a cloning vector which is no more pathogenic to the plants but is still able to use the mechanisms to deliver genes of our interest into a variety of plants. Similarly, retroviruses have also been disarmed and are now used to deliver desirable genes into animal cells.

(B) Normal E. coli cells naturally carry resistance genes against antibiotics such as ampicillin and tetracycline.

134824.sol:
According to NCERT, the 'ori' (origin of replication) sequence is responsible for controlling the copy number of the linked DNA. Thus, statement A is correct.

Normal E. coli cells do not carry resistance against antibiotics like ampicillin, tetracycline, kanamycin, or chloramphenicol. Thus, statement B is incorrect.

A cloning vector should preferably have a single recognition site for a commonly used restriction enzyme. The presence of multiple recognition sites generates several fragments, which complicates gene cloning. Thus, statement C is incorrect.

Selectable markers help in identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of transformants. Thus, statement D is correct.

Exactly two statements (A and D) are correct.

Answer: Only two

135101.subject: Zoology
135101.text: Why is the logistic growth model considered more realistic for most animal populations?
options: Because resources are finite and become limiting
Because it ignores birth and death rates
135101.sol: A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows initially a lag phase, followed by phases of acceleration and deceleration and finally an asymptote, when the population density reaches the carrying capacity. A plot of N in relation to time (t) results in a sigmoid curve. This type of population growth is called Verhulst-Pearl Logistic Growth (Figure 11.3) and is described by the following equation:dN/dt = rN(1-N/K)Where N = Population density at time tr = Intrinsic rate of natural increaseK = Carrying capacity<mark>Since resources for growth for most animal populations are finite and become limiting sooner or later, the logistic growth model is considered a more realistic one.</mark>Both the species benefit in mutualism and both lose in competition in their interactions with each other. In both parasitism and predation only one species benefits (parasite and predator, respectively) and the interaction is detrimental to the other species (host and prey, respectively). The interaction where one species is benefitted and the other is neither benefited or harmed is called commensalism. In amensalism on the other hand one species is harmed whereas the other is unaffected. Predation, parasitism and commensalism share a common characteristic– the interacting species live closely together.Therefore, competition is best defined as a process in which the fitness of one species (measured in terms of its ‘r’ the intrinsic rate of increase) is significantly lower in the presence of another species. It is relatively easy to demonstrate in laboratory experiments, as Gause and other experimental ecologists did, when resources are limited the competitively superior species will eventually eliminate the other species, but evidence for such competitive exclusion occurring in nature is not always conclusive.

135383.sol:
A. Sea anemone and clown fish: The clown fish gets protection from predators by living among the stinging tentacles of the sea anemone, while the anemone does not appear to derive any benefit nor is it harmed. This is commensalism $(+, 0)$.

B. Cuscuta and hedge plants: Cuscuta is a parasitic plant that derives its nutrition from the host hedge plant, harming it in the process. This is parasitism $(+, -)$.

C. Visiting flamingoes and resident fishes: In some shallow South American lakes, visiting flamingoes and resident fishes compete for their common food, the zooplankton. This is competition $(-, -)$.

D. Fig tree and wasp: The wasp pollinates the fig inflorescence while searching for suitable egg-laying sites, and in return, the fig offers developing seeds as food for the wasp larvae. This is mutualism $(+, +)$.

Therefore, the correct matching is A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

Answer: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
